# Spike 05-0 — how *This happened* is computed, and to what tolerance

**2026-09-21 · one read-only Opus agent · no file in the repository or any worktree was changed
outside `plans/`.** Every number below is printed by a script in
`plans/analysis/scripts/spike-05/observe/`, and the script is named beside it. The raw output of
every run is in `logs/` in that directory. No paid call, no server, no browser, no test suite.

**The words used here.** A *claim* is a yes/no proposition with a deadline; its number is the
chance it happens by that deadline. An *arrow* bends the *rate* at which its target happens from
the day its source happened plus a lag, with a shape (`step`, `impulse` with a half-life, `ramp`).
A *slice* is one of the K equal pieces the 60-day window is cut into; a claim's *arrival* is the
slice it first came true in, or "never". A *version* is one draw of the map's uncertain inputs; a
*range* is the 5th-to-95th percentile band of a number across versions. The *judge* is the exact
answer over the whole joint of arrival slices — computable only for four claims or fewer, which is
why accuracy is measured there and cost at twenty claims.

---

## The verdict in five lines

1. **Kill. No candidate passes the criterion as written**, and the binding constraint is not
   *This happened* at all — it is the forward pass that builds the tables, which all three
   candidates share and which nobody had costed. At twenty claims with two hundred versions it is
   **2.9 seconds**, against a 300 ms budget (`timing20.py`).
2. **The accuracy question has a clear winner.** A weighted forward sample with the exact yes/no
   solve used as a control variate — Kent's "exact core with a sampler on top", read literally —
   holds `.005` on **100.00%** of the adversarial set's *This happened* numbers at 200 000 worlds
   and **99.98%** at 50 000, against 93.4% for the design as proposed (`candidates.py`).
3. **Tolerance for the record:** `.005` for all three questions if the sampler lands; `.02` for no
   edit, `.03` for *Suppose this is true* and `.21` for *This happened* if the prior-timing tables
   are kept as they are.
4. **Versions per range: 2 000 is right, and only for narrow bands.** At the widths these maps
   produce, 2 000 versions still leaves the worst band end wandering `.0086`; 200 versions leaves
   it wandering `.0275`, which is one significant figure, not two (`versions.py`).
5. **Two findings worth more than the spike's own question.** Representing an arrival by the
   *middle* of its slice rather than its *end* — one line — cuts the grid error at 24 slices from
   a worst of `.0290` to `.0027` (`midpoint.py`). And the 0.5 ms that the engine design was sold on
   measured the elimination only: the factors were built from a random logistic function before the
   clock started (`analysis/scripts/engine/ve_cost.py:238-239`, clock at `:205`, factors at `:135`).

---

## 1. The baseline reproduces, digit for digit

The red team's own script was re-run unmodified, and the same sweep was re-run through this
spike's faster code. Both give the red team's table exactly.

**140 adversarial four-claim maps (seed 7), 17 queries each, 24 slices, arrival at the slice's
last day.** Gap between the design as proposed and the judge.

| query | numbers | mean | 99th percentile | worst | share off by more than .005 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no edit | 560 | .00027 | .0046 | .0175 | 0.9% |
| *Suppose this is true* | 4 480 | .00007 | .0015 | .0259 | 0.2% |
| *This happened* | 4 480 | .00127 | .0151 | **.2043** | **6.6%** |

Worst single number: trial 33, *This happened* on `c1`, read on `c3` — judge `.6155`, design
`.4112`.

*From `logs/baseline-redteam-attack2.log` (the red team's `attack2.py`, untouched) and
`logs/baseline.log` (`baseline.py`).*

**The faster code is the same code.** `spike_core.judge` shares each map's tables across its 17
queries instead of rebuilding them per query; `selfcheck.py` runs both side by side on 12 maps ×
17 queries and reports a worst difference of **0.000e+00** against `rt_core.exact_over_times` and
**1.6e-11** against `rt_core.binary`, at 167× the speed. Nothing in the red team's directory was
edited.

---

## 2. The candidates

All on the same 140 maps, 24 slices, judged against exact-over-times. The *This happened* column
is the one the criterion is about; `logs/candidates.log`, `logs/perday.log`.

### (a) A weighted forward sample — `sampler.py`

Worlds are drawn forward with arrival days, causes first. At the observed claim the world is not
thrown away: the claim is set to what was observed and the world's weight is multiplied by how
likely that was. Three variance reductions, all on: conditional sampling at the evidence, so no
world is wasted; the exact yes/no solve as a control variate — the same world is drawn twice, once
under the full time model and once under the design's own yes/no model, using the same random
number for each claim, so only the *difference* has to be sampled and it is added to an answer we
already know exactly; and one seeded stream in a fixed claim order, so two runs agree.

| *This happened*, 4 480 numbers | mean | 99th pct | worst | share > .005 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| read straight off the worlds, 50 000 | .00120 | .0051 | .0076 | 1.18% |
| read straight off the worlds, 200 000 | .00060 | .0026 | .0049 | 0.00% |
| **with the control variate, 50 000** | .00029 | .0021 | .0054 | **0.02%** |
| **with the control variate, 200 000** | .00015 | .0011 | .0020 | **0.00%** |
| with the control variate, 1 000 000 | .00007 | .0005 | .0011 | 0.00% |

It fixes the other two questions as well, because it targets the judge rather than the tables:

| | no edit (560) | *Suppose* (4 480) |
|---|---|---|
| the design's tables | worst .0175, 0.89% over .005 | worst .0259, 0.22% over .005 |
| sample + control variate, 50 000 | worst .0030, 0.00% | worst .0019, 0.00% |
| sample + control variate, 200 000 | worst .0013, 0.00% | worst .0014, 0.00% |

**Effective sample size** — how many equally-weighted worlds the weighted sample is worth — is
**96.7%** of the worlds drawn on average and **41.8%** at its worst across all 1 120 observations.
On the twenty-claim map it is 161 044 of 200 000 at 12 slices and 164 430 at 24
(`timing20.py`). The control variate buys a factor of about 2.4 on the 99th percentile, no more:
the two coupled worlds disagree 6.3% of the time on the hardest map, which is where the residual
variance lives (`probe_sampler.py`).

**Cost with a range (20 claims):** 190 ms for 200 000 worlds over all twenty claims at 12 slices,
**110 ms** over the twelve claims the evidence can reach (a claim cut off from the evidence keeps
its number exactly and need not be drawn — `engine20.reach_submap`). At 24 slices, 380 ms and
222 ms. That is *per version*, unless the correction is shared — see §5.

### (b) Accept the prior-timing tables — `spike_core.candidate_b`

The design as proposed, unchanged. Its honest tolerance is the baseline table in §1: **.02 for no
edit, .03 for *Suppose this is true*, .21 for *This happened***. A screen that prints two
significant figures beside `.21` of possible error on its second verb is printing a digit it does
not have. 6.63% of *This happened* numbers are off by more than `.005`, 0.56% by more than `.02`,
and 0.04% by more than `.05` (`tails.py`).

### (c) Re-cut the yes/no variable — `perday.py`, `hybrid.py`

Two readings were built, because the brief's phrase admits both.

**Per evidence day** (`perday.py`) — the literal reading. Answer the question once for each
possible day of the observed claim: pin that day, redo the forward pass, rebuild every table
downstream, solve; weight each answer by the likelihood of that day, which falls out of the solve.

**Widened variables** (`hybrid.py`) — give some claims their whole arrival slice as a variable
(K+1 values) instead of a yes/no. With nothing widened this is the design; with everything widened
it is the judge. Three rules were tried: widen only the observed claim; widen it and everything
upstream; widen everything the evidence can reach that some other claim reads.

| *This happened*, 4 480 numbers | mean | 99th pct | worst | share > .005 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| widen only the observed claim | .00119 | .0144 | .1968 | 5.98% |
| **per evidence day** | .00086 | .0127 | .0680 | 4.38% |
| widen it and its causes | .00040 | .0080 | .1963 | 1.85% |
| **widen everything the evidence reaches that is read** | .00002 | .0006 | .0063 | **0.07%** |

Only the last passes, and on a four-claim map it widens three claims of four — that is the judge
with one sink left over. Its cost is therefore the cost already measured and rejected for exact
inference over event times (`analysis/2026-09-21-digest-engine.md`: 0.7–7.8 s per range at twenty
claims). On the twenty-claim map measured here it widened only 5 of 20 claims and cost 25 ms per
version, but that is an accident of where the observation sat: `c6`'s only descendants are sinks,
which nobody reads. An observation higher up the map widens most of it.

**The per-day version can be worse than doing nothing.** On trial 65 it takes `c3` from the
design's `.5261` to `.4872` against a judge of `.5553` — it fixes the observed claim's own day and
leaves its *causes'* days alone, and the two errors stop cancelling (`worst_case.py`).

---

## 3. The kill criterion, applied literally

> *A candidate passes if it holds `.005` on 99% of the adversarial set **and** runs inside 300 ms
> on a 20-claim map (up to 3 causes per claim) for one world with its range.*

**Accuracy.** Passes: (a) with the control variate at 50 000 worlds or more (99.98%); (c) widened
to everything the evidence reaches (99.93%). Fails: (b) the tables as proposed (93.4%); (c) per
evidence day (95.6%); (c) with the smaller widenings.

**Milliseconds.** `timing20.py`, on a map from `ve_cost.layered_dag(20, 3, seed=1000)`, one
observation in force, all twenty marginals. The first three rows are the *shared* pass every
candidate pays for before anyone asks a question.

| | 1 version | 50 | 100 | 200 | 2 000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| calibrate the arrows | 28.0 | 95 | 192 | 384 | 3 905 |
| build the conditional tables | 12.9 | 628 | 1 217 | 2 438 | 24 831 |
| forward pass + yes/no tables | 0.9 | 14 | 28 | 56 | 570 |
| **shared by every candidate** | **41.8** | **737** | **1 437** | **2 879** | **29 318** |
| the exact yes/no solve, all marginals | 4.4 | 6.4 | 8.7 | 12.4 | 83 |
| **(b) total** | **46 ✓** | 744 | 1 446 | **2 891** | 29 401 |
| **(a) total, correction shared** | **161 ✓** | 856 | 1 555 | **3 002** | 29 527 |
| (a) total, correction redone per version | 161 ✓ | 6 367 | 12 340 | 24 992 | 281 761 |
| (c) per evidence day, every version | 101 ✓ | 3 709 | 7 406 | 14 611 | 152 022 |

*All milliseconds, 12 slices, eight integration points per slice. ✓ = inside 300 ms.*

At 24 slices — which §4 shows is the coarsest window worth having — the shared pass alone is
**208 ms for one version** and **9.6 s for fifty**.

**So: no candidate passes.** The nearest miss is candidate (a) with the correction shared across
versions: **3.0 s at 200 versions and 12 slices, ten times the budget**. And the miss is not in the
sampler, which is 110 ms; it is in the 2.9 s of table-building that candidate (b) pays too.

**What relaxing the criterion buys.**

| relaxation | what it buys | what it costs |
|---|---|---|
| budget **3 s** for one world with its range | (a) passes at 12 slices, 200 versions | 12 slices is 2.5% of *This happened* numbers off by more than .005 against the continuous answer, even with the middle-day fix (§4) — so the accuracy half then fails |
| budget **12 s** | (a) passes at 24 slices, 200 versions, with both halves honest | a range takes twelve seconds |
| accuracy **.02 on 99%** | (b) passes accuracy: its 99th percentiles are .0046 / .0015 / .0151 | nothing on the clock — (b) is still 2.9 s at 200 versions. Relaxing accuracy alone does not help |
| **50 versions** instead of 200 | shared pass falls to 737 ms | the band's ends wander `.0498` — one significant figure |
| **one claim's number at a time**, no range | 46 ms (b) / 161 ms (a) — both pass | there is no range, which is the product's honesty feature |

**The cheapest thing that has not been tried.** The tables are built by enumerating every
combination of the causes' arrival slices — 2 006 900 entries for this map at 24 slices — and then
*averaging* them. An average does not need every point. Replacing the enumeration with five
quadrature points per cause cuts it to 31 375 entries (64× fewer) and the whole forward pass from
208 ms to **38.5 ms** per version. It costs accuracy: *This happened* goes from 5.68% to 9.27% off
by more than .005, and no edit from 1.25% to 2.92% (`quad.py`, 60 maps). **And it is not available
to the winning candidate**, because a weighted forward sample needs a claim's table at whatever day
its causes actually landed on, not at five chosen days.

---

## 4. The grid nobody chose — the largest single number in this report

Every measurement above compares candidates *on the same grid*, so it is a fair comparison. But the
grid itself carries an error that the judge and every candidate share, and it is bigger than the
thing this spike was sent to measure.

A cause that arrives anywhere inside a slice has to be given a day. `rt_core` gives it the slice's
**last** day. That is late by half a slice on average — 1.25 days at 24 slices on a 60-day window.

Against a fine reference (60 slices, middle day), 10 maps, every query (`convergence.py`,
`midpoint.py`):

| the engine's window | *This happened*: 99th pct | worst | share > .005 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 slices, arrival at the slice's last day | .0547 | .0668 | 44.7% |
| 24 slices, last day | .0240 | .0290 | 27.8% |
| 60 slices, last day | .0093 | .0111 | 8.1% |
| **12 slices, arrival at the slice's middle** | .0068 | .0085 | 2.5% |
| **24 slices, middle** | **.0018** | **.0027** | **0.00%** |

**Twelve slices with the middle-day convention beats sixty slices with the last-day one, at a
twentieth of the cost.** This is a one-line change (`spike_core.representative_days`) and it costs
nothing.

It does **not** change which candidate wins. Re-run at 24 slices, middle day, judged there
(`midpoint.py`, 140 maps): the design's tables are still 6.07% off by more than .005 on *This
happened*, worst `.2095`; the sample with the control variate is still 0.00%, worst `.0021`. The
two defects are independent, and both are real.

*One caveat, honestly.* The *Suppose this is true* row of the grid comparison (5.6% over .005 at 24
slices middle day) is an artefact of this harness, not of the model: a supposition pins the claim
to the first slice, whose representative day differs between grids. A real implementation would pin
it to day zero. It is listed under what I did not check.

---

## 5. The worst remaining case, drawn

Trial 33 of the adversarial set is where the design is worst, and it is exactly the shape the red
team named: the observed claim is also a cause of another cause, and the reach is through impulse
arrows (`worst_case.py`).

```
   c0  ── deadline day 8.5, own chance .54
    │
    ├──► c1  deadline day 20.3, own chance .07
    │        from c0: .11 if that cause alone happens, lag 5.2 d, step
    │
    ├──► c2  deadline day 43.4, own chance .10
    │        from c0: .61, lag 3.1 d, step
    │        from c1: .33, lag 2.5 d, IMPULSE half-life 5.7 d
    │
    └──► c3  deadline day 56.0, own chance .09
             from c0: .11, lag 18.2 d, IMPULSE half-life 4.6 d
             from c2: .91, lag  5.2 d, IMPULSE half-life 12.4 d
             from c1: .03, lag 16.1 d, IMPULSE half-life 13.5 d
```

*This happened: `c1` is true.*

| | c0 | c1 | c2 | **c3** | worst gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| judge (exact over times) | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7283 | **.6155** | — |
| (b) prior-timing tables | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7269 | **.4112** | **.2043** |
| (c) widen the observed claim | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7282 | .4187 | .1968 |
| (c) widen it and its causes | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7283 | .4192 | .1963 |
| (c) per evidence day | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7282 | .6076 | .0079 |
| (c) widen everything read | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7283 | .6155 | .0000 |
| (a) sample 200 000, corrected | .6285 | 1.0000 | .7278 | .6159 | **.0005** |

Twenty points of probability, on the claim furthest downstream — the kind of claim a trade sits on.
The design prints `.41` where the answer is `.62`.

**The worst case candidate (a) has left** is not structural: trial 21, *This happened* on `c0`, read
on `c2` — judge `.4807`, sample `.4821`, gap `.0020` at 200 000 worlds, and it shrinks as the square
root of the count. **The worst case candidate (c) widened has left** is trial 124, gap `.0063`, and
it does not shrink with anything.

---

## 6. How many versions a range needs

`versions.py`. Twenty thousand versions of the twenty-claim map are solved exactly under an
observation; that pool stands in for "all versions". Then each smaller count is drawn from it two
thousand times and the band recomputed. *Wander* is half the middle 90% of where an end lands.

**Uncertain inputs drawn wide (a typical band .254 across):**

| versions | worst end wanders | as a share of the band | share of band ends inside .005 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | .0498 | 18% | 22.9% |
| 100 | .0390 | 14% | 29.6% |
| 200 | .0275 | 10% | 38.8% |
| 500 | .0176 | 6% | 55.6% |
| **2 000** | **.0086** | **3%** | **83.9%** |

**Uncertain inputs drawn narrow (a typical band .115 across):**

| versions | worst end wanders | as a share of the band | share inside .005 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | .0252 | 16% | 41.0% |
| 100 | .0192 | 12% | 53.0% |
| 200 | .0133 | 9% | 67.7% |
| 500 | .0086 | 6% | 86.5% |
| **2 000** | **.0046** | **3%** | **99.2%** |

**Recommendation: keep 2 000.** It is the smallest count that holds a narrow band's ends to two
significant figures, and even it does not hold a wide band's — a band `.25` across needs about
**6 000** versions for that, by the square-root rule the table obeys. The engine analyst's proposal
of "about 200 versions" is **wrong by an order of magnitude**: at 200 versions the 5th and 95th
ends wander by a tenth of the band's own width, which is one significant figure. The inner eight
worlds do go away — that saving is real — but it does not buy a smaller outer loop.

**Can the correction for *This happened* be shared across versions?** Yes, and it is the only thing
that makes candidate (a) affordable at all. On 8 maps × 200 versions, with the exact correction
(judge minus the design's answer) computed per version:

| | mean | 90th pct | worst |
|---|---|---|---|
| how big the correction is | .0005 | .0019 | .0041 |
| how much it moves from version to version (sd) | .0008 | .0025 | .0071 |
| how much the answer itself moves (sd) | .0616 | .1107 | .1234 |
| the ratio of those two | .011 | .030 | .096 |

The correction moves about **1% as much as the answer does**. Sharing one sampled correction across
every version adds about `.0013` to a band end on average and `.0117` at its worst. That is the
trade: one sample instead of two hundred, for a hundredth of an extra error on most numbers and a
tail that needs watching on maps where the correction is large. **These eight maps are four claims
each and the correction is small on them by construction** — on a map shaped like trial 33 the
correction is `.20`, and 1% of that is `.002`, still small, but nobody has measured the version-to-
version movement of a correction that size.

**Cost per version, and therefore per range** (candidate (a), 12 slices, shared correction):
2 879 ms of shared pass + 12 ms of solve for 200 versions + 110 ms for one sample = **3 002 ms**.
Per version that is 14.4 ms, and the sample is a fixed 110 ms however many versions there are.

---

## 7. The times the trade will read

Stack 06 reads a sample of worlds as `when` (the day each claim first came true, −1 for never) plus
a `weight`. Under *This happened* those days are only right if whatever produced them is. Red team
S2 flagged this and did not measure it. Here it is (`when_table.py`): 40 maps, every *This
happened* on every claim, 24 slices, 200 000 worlds, against the judge — which holds the whole
joint over days and is therefore exact.

*Total variation distance* below is half the sum of the absolute differences between two
distributions over days: 0 means identical, .10 means a tenth of the worlds would have to move.

| how each claim's day-it-happened spread compares with the judge's | mean | 99th pct | worst |
|---|---|---|---|
| **(a) weighted forward sample** | .0023 | .0047 | **.0064** |
| **(b) truths from the exact solve, days drawn forward under the prior** | .0104 | .0575 | **.2143** |

| how far the median day moves, in slices (one slice = 2.5 days) | mean | 99th pct | worst |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) weighted forward sample | .02 | 1 | 1 |
| (b) truths exact, days forward | .22 | 2 | **4 (ten days)** |

The design's own way of producing days — draw the truth pattern from the exact yes/no answer, then
walk the map drawing each true claim's day from tables built before the evidence — moves a claim's
median arrival by **up to ten days** under an observation. A stop-versus-target number computed
from those days is wrong by whatever ten days of path is worth. Candidate (a)'s days are right to
within sampling noise, and the same weighted sample serves both readers: one sampler, two uses.

---

## 8. The tolerance to write in the record

For `test_the_tables_agree_with_integrating_over_time` — the test whose enumerator is forbidden the
core's tables and is built from the arrow parameters alone.

**If the core is the weighted forward sample with the control variate, 200 000 worlds, 24 slices:**

| question | measured worst over 4 480–560 numbers | write |
|---|---|---|
| no edit | .0013 | **.005** |
| *Suppose this is true* | .0014 | **.005** |
| *This happened* | .0020 | **.005** |

At 50 000 worlds the measured worsts are `.0030`, `.0019`, `.0054`; `.005` then has no headroom on
*This happened* and the sample size must be part of the record.

**If the core is the prior-timing tables as proposed, 24 slices:**

| question | measured worst | write |
|---|---|---|
| no edit | .0175 | **.02** |
| *Suppose this is true* | .0259 | **.03** |
| *This happened* | .2043 | **.21** |

**Two conditions on either number.** The enumerator must run at the **same number of slices and the
same within-slice convention** as the core; a core at 24 slices judged by an enumerator at 60 with
a different convention differs by `.0290` on its own, which would swallow the tolerance. And the
sample must be seeded, so the test is deterministic.

---

## 9. What the decision record must say — sentences ready to paste

> **On what is exact.** *Suppose this is true* is exact: pin the claim, redo the forward pass, solve
> the yes/no network. Measured against an enumerator that integrates over the whole joint of event
> times, 4 480 numbers on 140 adversarial four-claim maps, the worst gap is `.0259` and 99.8% are
> inside `.005`.

> **On what is not.** *This happened* is not exact. Evidence moves *when* a cause happened as well
> as *whether* it did, and the yes/no tables were built from the timing the map had before the
> evidence arrived. Measured the same way, the worst gap is `.2043` and 6.6% of numbers are off by
> more than `.005`. It bites when the observed claim is itself a cause of another cause and the
> reach is through impulse arrows; a plain chain is exact.

> **On the cure.** *This happened* is answered by a weighted forward sample: worlds drawn forward
> with event days, the observed claim set to what was observed and the world weighted by how likely
> that was, with the exact yes/no answer used as a control variate so that only the correction is
> sampled. At 200 000 worlds the worst gap is `.0020` and no number is off by more than `.005`. The
> sample is seeded and reproducible. The same sample is what the trade reads as event days.

> **On the day a slice stands for.** An arrival inside a slice is taken to be at the slice's
> **middle**, not its end. At 24 slices this changes the worst gap against a fine reference from
> `.0290` to `.0027`; the last-day convention at 60 slices is worse than the middle-day convention
> at 12.

> **On the range.** A range is the 5th-to-95th percentile band across **2 000** versions of the map.
> The inner eight worlds are removed; the outer 2 000 are not. At 200 versions the band's ends
> wander by a tenth of the band's own width, which is one significant figure, not two.

> **On cost, and what is not yet settled.** A twenty-claim map with up to three causes per claim and
> 200 versions costs 3.0 seconds for one world with its range, of which 2.9 seconds is the forward
> pass that builds the tables and 0.11 seconds is the sample. The 300 ms budget is not met and this
> record does not claim it is. The costed ways down are a coarser window (measured: 12 slices costs
> 2.5% of *This happened* numbers more than `.005`), fewer integration points inside each slice
> (measured cost only, accuracy not measured), and replacing the table enumeration with a small
> quadrature (measured: 64× fewer entries, and it roughly doubles the share of numbers off by more
> than `.005`).

---

## 10. What I did not check

- **Anything above four claims, for accuracy.** The judge is not computable there. Every accuracy
  number in this report is from four-claim maps; the cost numbers are from twenty-claim maps and the
  two sets never meet.
- **Whether the correction stays shareable on a hard map.** The version-to-version movement of the
  correction was measured on eight four-claim maps where the correction is a few thousandths. On a
  map shaped like trial 33 the correction is `.20` and its movement across versions is unmeasured.
- **Fewer integration points inside a slice.** The cost was measured (one point instead of eight is
  4.9× faster on the table build); the accuracy was not, because the red team's calibration is fixed
  at eight and changing it means changing their code.
- **The *Suppose this is true* row of the grid comparison.** A supposition pins the claim to the
  first slice, whose representative day differs between grids, so that row measures the harness's
  pinning convention as much as the model. A real implementation pins to day zero.
- **A quadrature that is not stratified quantiles.** The five-point quadrature measured here is
  noisy in the number of points (eight points is not reliably better than three) because the points
  are rounded to slice indices. A better rule probably exists; I did not look for one.

- **Anything about state claims** — their on-time and off-time, and what they cost. That is the
  other half of stack 05's spike and it is a different agent's subject.
- **The stop-versus-target number itself.** §7 measures the error in the *days*; it does not push
  those days through a price path to a first-touch probability.
- **I ran no test suite, no server, no browser and no paid call.** Nothing in the repository outside
  `plans/` was changed.

---

## Owed once stack 04 has landed

Nothing. This spike wrote no product code and no chapter. The sentences in §9 belong to record 0016,
which the coordinator owns and which is not yet written.

153	- **Routes, seed and loop counts move off the always-on strip into a *Run details* section of the panel** (never a dialog). Both reviews asked independently; nothing is lost, it is one click away. *Recommended.*

167	| Cut from the plan: a one-call skeleton, an ensemble, *Release*/undo, a slider, the pastcast, `refine`, feedback loops, the simulation probe, expected shortfall and ruin, a fifth kind of claim | `design-after-midpoint-review.md` §7, each with its reason | Name it |

# Design after the midpoint reviews — what changes, what stays, and why

**2026-09-21 · coordinator's synthesis, revised after one adversarial pass · KENT ANSWERED every question it raised the same evening (`notes/2026-09-21-decisions-after-review.md`, R1–R17).** Where this page says *proposed* or offers options, read the decisions note for what he chose: **events and states (R2); the path product replaced (R3); the spread lands with a disagreeing row greyed, not dropped (R4); one freeze after the flip, then all four examples recorded once (R5, R9); one plain probability per arrow (R6); `36%`, with the formatter moved to the browser first (R17 — this overturns §2.5's "formatting stays in `domain/`").** The decision records themselves are still written `proposed` and accepted by him before code is built against them. **Where it comes from.** Two independent reviews (`review/`, `review2/`) were digested by four read-only Opus analysts, each re-checking every finding against today's code (`main` = `48eb562`): `analysis/2026-09-21-digest-{engine,finance,generation,craft}.md`. A fifth agent then attacked the first draft of this page: `analysis/2026-09-21-red-team.md`. **Those five reports hold the evidence** — file and line, measurements — and their scripts are kept in `analysis/scripts/`. This page holds the conclusions, and says where an analyst was overruled. Kent's four answers to `review2` (2026-09-21) are treated as direction: **an exact core with a sampler on top · keep the time model and make it sound · land what is open, then finance before more generation · revisit generation.**

**The bar** (Kent, 2026-09-21): rewrites of merged work are allowed *"but should be weighed against a high standard of quality improvement … the best tradeoffs in terms of work required versus improvements made."* And: the spec stays a first-class book; shorten it *where warranted*, not as a maxim.

**How sure this page is.** §2 rests on prototypes of a few hundred lines on maps of five claims or fewer, not on the product. It therefore ends in a **spike with a kill criterion**, not a commitment. §3 is design on open ground. §4 rests on measurements of one real recording and three kept runs. §5 was judged from code and five screenshots, not from a running browser.

---

## 1. The verdict in six lines

1. **The foundations stand.** Branches as patches, the validator that rejects and never repairs, locality, the typed wire, replay, the canvas and its keyboard: both reviews, four analysts and the red team say keep them. Nothing here is a rewrite of the product.
2. **The arithmetic does not.** Three defects reproduce on today's `main`, on the demo map, under 100% coverage. The band has an independent cross-check; **the likelihoods have none, and nothing independent runs under an edit** — that gap let all three through.
3. **The cure is a change of question, not a bigger sampler:** a claim's number becomes *the chance it happens by its deadline*; *whether* is solved exactly; *when* is sampled forward. It is right for *Suppose* to four decimal places. It is **not yet right for *This happened*** — the first draft of this page said "exact" there and the red team measured .12 of error. The engine stack opens with a spike that settles that before anything is built on it.
4. **The brief ends in a trade and the trade has no code.** Stack 06 builds it in four pull requests behind one narrow contract with the engine.
5. **Every change to what we ask the model for lands once, after the engine is proven**, then Hormuz is recorded once. The payoff `kind` fix waits for that.
6. **Less is built, on purpose** — §7.

---

## 2. The engine — what a number means, and how it is worked out

### 2.1 The three defects (all on `main` today; re-run by the coordinator, an analyst and the red team)

| | What happens | Root cause |
|---|---|---|
| **An observation never reaches a cause.** | Two claims, A → B. *This happened* on B leaves A at `.3000`; the right answer is `.4562`. It prints the same number as *Suppose this is true*. | The engine keeps each claim's worked-out likelihood and throws away the coin flip. For a claim with no causes that likelihood is the same in every world, so filtering worlds by the observation cannot move it (`propagation.py:1470`). |
| **Endings are deaf to half their causes.** | On Hormuz, supposing the insurance premium (C) or OPEC+ restraint (R) moves Brent (B) by .06–.17 and moves both endings by `0.0000`. | A trigger arrow reads its source on the day the source's **earliest** incoming arrow lands. For B that is day 2; C's push lands on day 7 and R's on day 5 — inside B's own series, invisible to B's outgoing arrows (`propagation.py:806-843`, `:1463`). |
| **A claim nobody believes deletes a supposition.** | Insert a claim with a prior of `.001` and an arrow of `−0.01` into a supposed claim: the tile never reads *Supposed*, on any day. | A supposition ends on a calendar worked out from the map's shape. It never asks whether the opposing cause happened, or how hard it pushes (`propagation.py:888-948`). |

Also true: the range under an observation can be made entirely of coin flips (`.157` wide with every input frozen); and a merged test (`test_an_observation_moves_a_cause_even_when_no_arrow_pushes`) enshrines sampling noise as required behaviour.

**A repair inside today's engine was costed and rejected** (engine analyst §3a): fixing the first defect there destroys the range or multiplies latency by thirty; fixing the second makes the settled day random, which the grid, the day-states, retraction and the locality proof are all built on. It *is* the reformulation.

### 2.2 The design — proposed record 0016

**A claim's number is the chance it resolves YES by its own deadline.** That is what the sentence on the tile already says. It is not a snapshot read on one day, and an event that has happened never un-happens.
=== SECTION 4 ===
## 4. Generation — settle the shapes once, after the engine is proven

Measured on the committed recording and three kept runs (generation analyst §0) — several of `review2`'s claims are out of date:

- **The map is not a tree.** 1.12–1.37 arrows per claim, claims with two and four causes, `LinkProposal` used in 2 of 20 and 7 of 28 accepted proposals. The *quality* case for drafting a whole map in one call is gone; its remaining case is speed, and `review2`'s "3 minutes, $0.70" is, against the measured price and pace of a call, roughly 2× optimistic on time and 3× on money.
- **Search is the clock.** A call that searches takes 3–4× the seconds. 93 searches bought five base rates on eighteen claims; three of the five are `0/2`, `2/3`, `1/1`.
- **The recorded map has no arrow that pushes down.** The answer shape *allows* one (the `strength` field's description says so) and one kept run drew three; but the standing text never asks *what would stop this step*, and the scripted insert — which is adversarial — drew three negative arrows at once. The cheap fix is a question, not a shape.
- **`review2`'s evidence check cannot be built** — the search tool returns encrypted content and the structured answer carries no citations. `review/`'s version can: a quoted passage and the role it plays.

**One shape freeze, then one paid re-record of Hormuz — and the freeze comes AFTER the engine's flip, not before it** (the first draft had it before; the red team showed three fingerprint moves would then have landed after the paid run — red team M6). Everything that changes the standing prompt or the answer shapes moves the prompt fingerprint and makes the recording stale, so it all goes together, once the engine has proven what it needs to be told:

- **One number per arrow, not a free-floating strength — and it must mean one thing** (red team M7). The claim's own number is restated as what the code has always used it as: *the chance it happens by its deadline if none of the causes on this map happens*. Each arrow carries `p_if_only_this_cause`: *the chance the effect happens by that same deadline if this cause happens on the first day of the window and no other cause on the map does.* Our code derives the arrow's weight. Removed: the elicited `strength`, and with it "+1 triples the odds" — a number we wrote inside a prompt.
- `persistence: event | state` on a claim — **if** Kent takes option (i) of §2.3.
- `quote` and `role` on a source (`mechanism · magnitude · timing · resolution · instrument`); `what_would_change_my_mind` on an arrow.
- `kind` required on both payoffs — **the branch already written, held until now**; a price ending's expected `move` as a range (free here; a second paid re-record if added later).
- Sentences asking what would *stop* each step and what would *falsify* each ending; a venue contract named where a real one exists.
- No search on the first call (7 s to a first tile, measured) and five claims at once; research a base rate only where a reference class can exist, and drop a count under five; a price ending's instrument must appear in its own test.
- Three that never touch the fingerprint and can go earlier: a refusal says whether *our rules* or *the answer* caused it; dropped sources and dropped base rates reach the wire; one clarifying clause on PRD anti-pattern 2 (a first draft of a map is not a re-prompt after an edit).

**Record on the branch and commit the new recording and cassettes in the same pull request** — "no search on the first call" changes the request body the cassettes match on but *not* the fingerprint, so merging the code first would leave `main` with a green hash over a recording of behaviour the program no longer has.

**The existing `hormuz.jsonl` is valid against `main`** (fingerprint byte-identical, checked by the red team) **and lands as it is.** The payoff defect is latent — the model filled the field in all eleven trades.

**Not planned** (each was in the first draft as "later, gated"; the red team is right that a gate is still a line on the plan): drafting a skeleton in one streamed call — three sessions for speed the recorded demo does not need; an ensemble for numbers — FR-8 and record 0015 forbid it in so many words, and the one condition that reopens it is the pastcast, which is cut. Both go on the *what I would do next* page. **Kept untouched:** three silent retries; one walk-driver; every refusal an event; provenance decided by us.

---

The engine stack opens with a spike that settles that before anything is built on it.
4. **The brief ends in a trade and the trade has no code.** Stack 06 builds it in four pull requests behind one narrow contract with the engine.
5. **Every change to what we ask the model for lands once, after the engine is proven**, then Hormuz is recorded once. The payoff `kind` fix waits for that.
6. **Less is built, on purpose** — §7.

---

## 2. The engine — what a number means, and how it is worked out

### 2.1 The three defects (all on `main` today; re-run by the coordinator, an analyst and the red team)

| | What happens | Root cause |
|---|---|---|
| **An observation never reaches a cause.** | Two claims, A → B. *This happened* on B leaves A at `.3000`; the right answer is `.4562`. It prints the same number as *Suppose this is true*. | The engine keeps each claim's worked-out likelihood and throws away the coin flip. For a claim with no causes that likelihood is the same in every world, so filtering worlds by the observation cannot move it (`propagation.py:1470`). |
| **Endings are deaf to half their causes.** | On Hormuz, supposing the insurance premium (C) or OPEC+ restraint (R) moves Brent (B) by .06–.17 and moves both endings by `0.0000`. | A trigger arrow reads its source on the day the source's **earliest** incoming arrow lands. For B that is day 2; C's push lands on day 7 and R's on day 5 — inside B's own series, invisible to B's outgoing arrows (`propagation.py:806-843`, `:1463`). |
| **A claim nobody believes deletes a supposition.** | Insert a claim with a prior of `.001` and an arrow of `−0.01` into a supposed claim: the tile never reads *Supposed*, on any day. | A supposition ends on a calendar worked out from the map's shape. It never asks whether the opposing cause happened, or how hard it pushes (`propagation.py:888-948`). |

Also true: the range under an observation can be made entirely of coin flips (`.157` wide with every input frozen); and a merged test (`test_an_observation_moves_a_cause_even_when_no_arrow_pushes`) enshrines sampling noise as required behaviour.

**A repair inside today's engine was costed and rejected** (engine analyst §3a): fixing the first defect there destroys the range or multiplies latency by thirty; fixing the second makes the settled day random, which the grid, the day-states, retraction and the locality proof are all built on. It *is* the reformulation.

### 2.2 The design — proposed record 0016

**A claim's number is the chance it resolves YES by its own deadline.** That is what the sentence on the tile already says. It is not a snapshot read on one day, and an event that has happened never un-happens.
=== SECTION 4 ===
## 4. Generation — settle the shapes once, after the engine is proven

Measured on the committed recording and three kept runs (generation analyst §0) — several of `review2`'s claims are out of date:

- **The map is not a tree.** 1.12–1.37 arrows per claim, claims with two and four causes, `LinkProposal` used in 2 of 20 and 7 of 28 accepted proposals. The *quality* case for drafting a whole map in one call is gone; its remaining case is speed, and `review2`'s "3 minutes, $0.70" is, against the measured price and pace of a call, roughly 2× optimistic on time and 3× on money.
- **Search is the clock.** A call that searches takes 3–4× the seconds. 93 searches bought five base rates on eighteen claims; three of the five are `0/2`, `2/3`, `1/1`.
- **The recorded map has no arrow that pushes down.** The answer shape *allows* one (the `strength` field's description says so) and one kept run drew three; but the standing text never asks *what would stop this step*, and the scripted insert — which is adversarial — drew three negative arrows at once. The cheap fix is a question, not a shape.
- **`review2`'s evidence check cannot be built** — the search tool returns encrypted content and the structured answer carries no citations. `review/`'s version can: a quoted passage and the role it plays.

**One shape freeze, then one paid re-record of Hormuz — and the freeze comes AFTER the engine's flip, not before it** (the first draft had it before; the red team showed three fingerprint moves would then have landed after the paid run — red team M6). Everything that changes the standing prompt or the answer shapes moves the prompt fingerprint and makes the recording stale, so it all goes together, once the engine has proven what it needs to be told:

- **One number per arrow, not a free-floating strength — and it must mean one thing** (red team M7). The claim's own number is restated as what the code has always used it as: *the chance it happens by its deadline if none of the causes on this map happens*. Each arrow carries `p_if_only_this_cause`: *the chance the effect happens by that same deadline if this cause happens on the first day of the window and no other cause on the map does.* Our code derives the arrow's weight. Removed: the elicited `strength`, and with it "+1 triples the odds" — a number we wrote inside a prompt.
- `persistence: event | state` on a claim — **if** Kent takes option (i) of §2.3.
- `quote` and `role` on a source (`mechanism · magnitude · timing · resolution · instrument`); `what_would_change_my_mind` on an arrow.
- `kind` required on both payoffs — **the branch already written, held until now**; a price ending's expected `move` as a range (free here; a second paid re-record if added later).
- Sentences asking what would *stop* each step and what would *falsify* each ending; a venue contract named where a real one exists.
- No search on the first call (7 s to a first tile, measured) and five claims at once; research a base rate only where a reference class can exist, and drop a count under five; a price ending's instrument must appear in its own test.
- Three that never touch the fingerprint and can go earlier: a refusal says whether *our rules* or *the answer* caused it; dropped sources and dropped base rates reach the wire; one clarifying clause on PRD anti-pattern 2 (a first draft of a map is not a re-prompt after an edit).

**Record on the branch and commit the new recording and cassettes in the same pull request** — "no search on the first call" changes the request body the cassettes match on but *not* the fingerprint, so merging the code first would leave `main` with a green hash over a recording of behaviour the program no longer has.

**The existing `hormuz.jsonl` is valid against `main`** (fingerprint byte-identical, checked by the red team) **and lands as it is.** The payoff defect is latent — the model filled the field in all eleven trades.

**Not planned** (each was in the first draft as "later, gated"; the red team is right that a gate is still a line on the plan): drafting a skeleton in one streamed call — three sessions for speed the recorded demo does not need; an ensemble for numbers — FR-8 and record 0015 forbid it in so many words, and the one condition that reopens it is the pastcast, which is cut. Both go on the *what I would do next* page. **Kept untouched:** three silent retries; one walk-driver; every refusal an event; provenance decided by us.

## 1. The definition, in eight lines

1. **A claim is an event or a state. An event has one time — the day it happens. A state
   has two — the day it switches *on* and the day it switches *off*.** Both come out of
   the same machinery: a rate, integrated over the claim's own window.
2. **A state's on-rate is bent by its causes exactly as an event's rate is. Its off-rate
   starts at zero and is the sum of its ending causes.** Nothing on the map that can end it
   means it does not end — so **no second elicited number is needed**, and a state that
   decayed on its own would be decaying for a reason nobody could name.
3. **The sign of an arrow decides which rate it bends.** An arrow whose elicited number is
   *above* the claim's own number helps, and bends the on-rate. One *below* it ends, and
   bends the off-rate. **No new field on the arrow.**
4. **One on-off interval, never a second.** A state that comes back is a second claim. What
   this gives up: *the strait reopens again in December* needs its own box.
5. **The number answers one question: is it holding on its deadline?** On by the deadline
   and not yet off. On the worked map in §3 the tile reads
   *"17% — the chance this still holds on 1 November"* where an event's reads *"35% —
   the chance this happens by 1 November"*. **Two words differ**, and under R17 the
   sentence is composed in the browser, so it is a one-file change.
6. **A `sustain` arrow reads its source's interval** — it pushes from the on time plus its
   lag until the off time, and is dead after. **A `trigger` arrow reads the on time alone**
   and keeps pushing afterwards. `trigger` is legal out of both; `sustain` only out of a
   state. That is the one new validity rule.
7. ***Suppose this is true* pins a state on from its date and never off. *This happened* on
   a date says it was holding on that date.** Both are the surgery an event already gets:
   pin the time, cut the incoming arrows.
8. **The per-day series is the chance it is holding on day *t*.** An event's only rises. A
   state's rises and falls. This is exactly red-team M4, answered: the field keeps its type
   and gains a second meaning, told apart by which kind of claim it belongs to.

### Why the sign is allowed to decide — measured

Line 3 is the one place a second field was on the table: an explicit *"this arrow bends the
on-rate / the off-rate"*. Two things had to be shown before deriving it from the sign was
safe. First, that the **other** reading — a negative arrow bending the on-rate down, which
is what a negative arrow into an *event* does — cannot tell the Hormuz story. Same map,
same elicited numbers, only this rule changed *(script: `hormuz.py` §D)*:

| the strike arrow bends | the state, lane open, no strike | after the strike | the fall |
|---|---|---|---|
| **the off-rate (proposed)** | .8291 | **.0533** | **−.7757** |
| the on-rate (alternative) | .9298 | .7460 | −.1838 |

Once the lane is already open the on-rate has done its work, so making it smaller barely
moves anything: a strike that plainly closes the strait moves the claim everything hangs on
by **18 points instead of 78**. That is the same shape as the defect record 0017 exists to
remove — a later event that plainly matters changing plainly nothing. **Bending the
off-rate is the only one of the two that can take something already holding and stop it.**

Second, what deriving it costs, stated: **you cannot say *"peace talks make it less likely
to stop"***. A cause that helps can only make a state **start**, never make it **last
longer**. Nothing in the Hormuz story wants to say that, and the alternative is a field the
model must fill, a prompt sentence, a validity rule and a second item in the shape freeze.
If Kent wants the fourth combination it is a one-value-to-two-value change in the
calibration and about a session.

1	"""What we say to the model. Product text, written once, sent unchanged.
2	
3	Two halves, and the split is the whole design.
4	
5	**The standing half** never changes between calls: what we are building, what a
6	claim is, what an arrow is, and the three things an answer may be. It is the
7	first thing in every request, byte for byte, so the service can recognise it and
8	charge a tenth of the price for reading it again. One stray timestamp, one
9	dictionary written out in a different order, and that saving is gone with no
10	error to tell you — so this half is a constant in this file, and the varying half
11	is assembled below it and always comes after.
12	
13	**The varying half** is the map as it stands and the one claim we are asking
14	about. It is written as sorted text so that the same map always produces the same
15	bytes, which is also what lets a recorded run be compared with a live one.
16	
17	Three rules about this text
18	---------------------------
19	- **It is product text.** A person reads it in review, the way any other words on
20	  screen are read. No jargon, no shorthand, no word the interface does not use.
21	- **It contains no number nobody worked out.** Not an example likelihood, not an
22	  example push, not an example delay. A number in a prompt is an anchor the model
23	  copies, and a copied number cannot say where it came from.
24	- **It never asks the model to do our job.** Nothing here says "do not draw a
25	  loop", "do not reuse an identifier" or "mark the arrow documented if you cite
26	  something". Whether a map is legal is decided by `katalyst.domain` over the map
27	  a proposal would leave behind, and a prompt that asked for the same thing would
28	  teach the model to aim at passing our checks rather than at being right — and
29	  when the two disagree, nobody could tell which was obeyed.
30	
31	What this file must never do
32	----------------------------
33	- Never put the time, a run's identifier, or anything else that changes per call
34	  into the standing half.
35	- Never tell a later call what an earlier proposal was refused for. A refusal is
36	  shown to the person and never enters a prompt, on any call.
37	- Never talk to the network, mint anything, or decide anything.
38	"""
39	
40	import hashlib
41	import json
42	from datetime import date
43	
44	from katalyst.domain import Graph, PropositionId
45	from katalyst.domain.validity import TERMINAL_KINDS
46	
47	STANDING_TEXT = """\
48	You are helping somebody think through what an event they expect would set off,
49	step by step, until the story reaches something they could actually trade.
50	
51	You do this one piece at a time, and you will be asked two kinds of question.
52	
53	The first kind hands you a sentence somebody typed and asks you to write it as a
54	claim. That is the whole job on that call: one claim, done properly. It is worth
55	as much care as any other, because everything after it hangs off it.
56	
57	The second kind shows you the map as it stands, points at one claim on it, and
58	asks for the single next piece. Somebody watches the map grow as your answers
59	arrive, so a small, well-argued piece beats a large, vague one.
60	
61	What a claim is.
62	A claim is something that will be plainly true or false by a date, settled by a
63	named source. "The drug pipeline looks healthy" is not a claim, because two
64	honest people will never agree on whether it happened. "The United States Food
65	and Drug Administration grants full approval to at least one new obesity
66	treatment, listed in its own approvals database, before the thirty-first of
67	March" is a claim, because they will.
68	
69	A claim stands on its own. Write it as a plain statement of the thing that
70	happens, with no lead-in and no explanation attached: "Retail pharmacy stocks of
71	the treatment run short in at least twenty states." Not "With approval granted,
72	retail stocks run short", not "Once the approval lands, stocks run short", not
73	"As a result, stocks run short". The *because* is not part of the claim — it
74	belongs in the arrow that reaches it, and putting it in both means a box on the
75	screen that argues with itself. Somebody reads this claim on a tile, on its own,
76	with nothing around it, and it has to make sense there.
77	
78	Every claim carries the test that settles it, the name of whoever applies that
79	test, and the day by which the answer is known. The test is written so that two
80	people reading it would reach the same answer: a number, a threshold, a source
81	that publishes it. "At least fourteen consecutive days" is a test. "Returns to
82	normal" is not. The judge is a named publication, exchange, agency or venue —
83	"the Baltic Exchange daily assessments", not "the news", and never a placeholder.
84	
85	Start from the outside, then come inside.
86	Before you say how likely a claim is, find out how often this kind of thing has
87	happened before. **Search for it.** Say what set of past cases you counted,
88	precisely enough that somebody else could count it again, how many of them came
89	out the way this claim describes, and out of how many.
90	
91	Stop searching as soon as you have a countable set with a page behind it. If you
92	cannot find one — some claims genuinely have no honest reference class — leave
93	the count out altogether. A count you cannot point at a page for is worse than no
94	count: it looks like a measurement and it is a memory, and we will drop it.
95	
96	Then say how likely this particular claim is, with the honest range around it —
97	wide when you are reaching, narrow when you are on familiar ground. The range is
98	how sure you are of your own number.
99	
100	What an arrow is.
101	An arrow is a claim about a mechanism: this happening moves the odds of that.
102	It says which way and how hard it pushes, how many whole days it takes to arrive,
103	and what it does over time — a spike that fades, a switch that stays on, or a
104	climb that builds and then holds. It says whether the push survives its cause
105	going away: a toppled domino stays down, while an apple only stays up while the
106	desk is under it. And it says, in one to three sentences, why the mechanism is
107	real. An arrow with a number and no reason is worth nothing to the person reading
108	it. This is where the *because* goes.
109	
110	Where the backing comes from.
111	Cite only addresses the search returned to you in this same call. If you did not
112	search, or nothing useful came back, cite nothing and say what you know in the
113	reason instead. An empty list of citations is an honest answer we can show. An
114	address you are recalling rather than reading is not backing, and we will not
115	treat it as backing.
116	
117	How a story ends, and how it gets there.
118	Most pieces are steps: something that happens on the way, which causes the next
119	thing. Give the story its next step and let it run — a map that jumps from the
120	first claim to a trade has skipped the argument that makes the trade worth
121	anything.
122	
123	An ending is different, and it is narrower than it sounds. A claim is an ending
124	you could trade **only when its own test is a price or a contract outcome
125	somebody could take a position on today**: a named contract at a named venue with
126	the side you would take, or an instrument with a direction and how far you expect
127	its price to move. "Storage across Europe is at least eighty per cent full" is a
128	step, however tradeable it feels — what settles it is a storage figure, not a
129	price. "The front-month contract settles below ninety" is an ending, because what
130	settles it is the price itself.
131	
132	The other ending is a plain statement that there is nothing to trade here, and
133	why. Both are good endings. An ending that trails off into prose is not.
134	
135	What an answer is.
136	Exactly one of three things:
137	  a new claim, together with the one arrow that reaches it from a claim already
138	  on the map;
139	  an arrow between two claims that are both already on the map;
140	  or a note that this part of the story is finished, with one sentence saying
141	  why.
142	
143	You never name a new claim with anything but its words. The short names in the
144	map we show you are ours; point at one when you name a cause, and never invent
145	another.
146	"""
147	"""The standing half of every request: the same bytes on every call, for ever.
148	
149	Kept as one constant rather than assembled, so that a reader can see the whole of
150	what we say to a model in one place and so that nothing can quietly vary.
151	"""
152	
153	
154	def prompt_hash() -> str:
155	    """Return one string that changes whenever what we ask for changes.
156	
157	    A recording of a run is only worth playing back while the questions behind it
158	    still hold. This fingerprint covers both halves of a question that can drift
159	    without anybody noticing: the standing text above, and the shapes an answer
160	    must fit. Change a sentence or add a field, and every recording made before
161	    the change can be told apart from one made after.
162	
163	    The shapes it covers are the ones **as they go out over the wire**, not as
164	    they are written here. The client library tidies a shape before sending it,
165	    and what the model was actually asked for is the tidied one — so if that
166	    tidying ever changes, every recording made before it can be told from every
167	    recording made after, which is exactly what this is for.
168	
169	    It deliberately does **not** cover the varying half. That differs on every
170	    call by design, and folding it in would make the fingerprint useless.
171	
172	    Returns:
173	        The fingerprint as plain hexadecimal, the same on every machine.
174	    """
175	    # Imported inside the function rather than at the top of the file, because the
176	    # seam reads this module and this line reads the seam. Both are fully loaded
177	    # by the time anybody asks for a fingerprint.
178	    #
179	    # It asks the seam for the shapes rather than naming them, so this file still
180	    # does not know what the wire forced on them — the envelope is the seam's
181	    # business and nothing outside it names it (2026-09-20).
182	    from katalyst.engine.client import what_goes_out
183	
184	    shapes = json.dumps(what_goes_out(), sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
185	    return hashlib.sha256((STANDING_TEXT + shapes).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()
186	
187	
188	def starting_question(sentence: str, *, is_the_hypothesis: bool, today: date) -> str:
189	    """Ask for one sentence a person typed, written as a claim anybody could settle.
190	
191	    Asked once for the sentence the map starts from, once more for the place the
192	    person asked whether it gets to, and once for a claim they ask to add later.
193	    Nothing exists yet the first two times, so there is no map to show.
194	
195	    **It asks for each part separately, and it says what a bad answer looks
196	    like.** The first measured run came back with a test reading `"Res "` and a
197	    judge reading `"x "`, in seven seconds, and the map's own rules accepted both
198	    because neither is empty. Nothing downstream can catch a two-character test
199	    without grading prose, so the fix is here: ask for one thing at a time, say
200	    what each one is for, and show the shape of an answer that is not good enough.
201	
202	    Args:
203	        sentence: What the person typed, unchanged.
204	        is_the_hypothesis: True for the sentence the map starts from, False for
205	            the place they asked whether it gets to. It changes one sentence of
206	            framing and nothing else.
207	        today: The day this run is happening. A person writing "next week" means a
208	            week from a particular day, and nothing else in the request says
209	            which. It sits here, in the varying half, and never in the standing
210	            half, where it would change the bytes the service recognises on every
211	            single run.
212	
213	    Returns:
214	        The varying half of the request, as plain text.
215	    """
216	    opening = (
217	        "Somebody typed this, and expects it to happen:"
218	        if is_the_hypothesis
219	        else "Somebody asked whether their expectation gets them to this:"
220	    )
221	    lines = [
222	        _today(today),
223	        "",
224	        opening,
225	        "",
226	        f"    {sentence.strip()}",
227	        "",
228	        "Write it as one claim. Take the care you would take over any other: "
229	        "everything else on this map hangs off this one, and a claim nobody can "
230	        "settle makes every number below it meaningless.",
231	        "",
232	        "Keep their meaning. Do not make it more modest or more dramatic than they "
233	        "did, and do not answer a question they did not ask.",
234	        "",
235	        "Four things, each one properly:",
236	        "",
237	        "  The claim itself, as a plain standalone statement of what happens. No "
238	        "lead-in, no explanation, nothing about what caused it.",
239	        "",
240	        "  The test that settles it — a number, a threshold, a count, something "
241	        "published. Written so that two people reading it reach the same answer. "
242	        "If your test is shorter than the claim, it is not a test.",
243	        "",
244	        "  The name of whoever applies that test: a publication, an exchange, an "
245	        "agency, a venue. A real one, by name.",
246	        "",
247	        "  The day by which the answer is known, worked out from today's date "
248	        "above and from what they said.",
249	        "",
250	        "Then search for how often this kind of thing has happened before, and give "
251	        "the count and the set you counted if you find one you can point at a page "
252	        "for. Leave it out if you cannot. Then how likely this one is, with the "
253	        "honest range around it.",
254	    ]
255	    if not is_the_hypothesis:
256	        lines += [
257	            "",
258	            "Write only this claim. Whether anything leads to it is the question "
259	            "they asked, not something to answer here.",
260	        ]
261	    return "\n".join(lines)
262	
263	
264	def adding_question(graph: Graph, sentence: str, *, today: date) -> str:
265	    """Ask for a claim somebody wants to add to a map, written so it can be checked.
266	
267	    The first half of *Add a claim*. It is the starting question with the map
268	    shown beside it, because a claim being added to a story should be written in
269	    the terms that story already uses — the same dates, the same judges, the same
270	    level of detail — and because the words it uses are what the arrows will hang
271	    off.
272	
273	    **It needs no shape of its own.** What comes back is a starting claim: the
274	    thing that happens, the test, the judge, the date. Its arrows are asked for
275	    afterwards, one per call, by the ordinary machinery.
276	
277	    Args:
278	        graph: The map the claim is going onto.
279	        sentence: What the person typed.
280	        today: The day this is happening.
281	
282	    Returns:
283	        The varying half of the request, as plain text.
284	    """
285	    return "\n".join(
286	        [
287	            _today(today),
288	            "",
289	            "Here is a map somebody has built. The short name in front of each claim is ours.",
290	            "",
291	            _map_as_text(graph),
292	            "",
293	            "They want to add this to it:",
294	            "",
295	            f"    {sentence.strip()}",
296	            "",
297	            "Write it as one claim, in the terms this map already uses — the same "
298	            "kind of test, the same kind of judge, dates in the same window. Keep "
299	            "their meaning; do not answer a question they did not ask, and do not "
300	            "say anything here about what it would cause. That comes next, and "
301	            "separately.",
302	            "",
303	            "The claim itself as a plain standalone statement; the test that settles "
304	            "it; the name of whoever applies that test; the day the answer is known. "
305	            "Then search for how often this kind of thing has happened before, and "
306	            "give the count only if you can point at a page for it. Then how likely "
307	            "it is, with the range around it.",
308	        ]
309	    )
310	
311	
312	def joining_question(graph: Graph, added: PropositionId, *, today: date) -> str:
313	    """Ask for one arrow between the newly added claim and the map it joined.
314	
315	    The second half of *Add a claim*, asked over and over until the model says
316	    there is nothing more. **It needs no shape of its own either**: what comes
317	    back is an ordinary arrow between two claims already on the map, which is
318	    exactly what this is once the claim has been added.
319	
320	    The new claim is named in the question rather than pinned by a field, because
321	    a field would be a fourth shape for something the words can say perfectly
322	    well — and a shape is forever while a sentence is not.
323	
324	    Args:
325	        graph: The map, with the new claim already on it.
326	        added: The claim that was just added.
327	        today: The day this is happening.
328	
329	    Returns:
330	        The varying half of the request, as plain text.
331	    """
332	    claims = {one.id: one for one in graph.propositions}
333	    joined = sorted(
334	        f"{claims[one.source].claim} -> {claims[one.target].claim}"
335	        for one in graph.links
336	        if added in (one.source, one.target)
337	    )
338	    lines = [
339	        _today(today),
340	        "",
341	        "Here is the map as it stands. The short name in front of each claim is "
342	        "ours; use one when you name either end of an arrow.",
343	        "",
344	        _map_as_text(graph),
345	        "",
346	        f"The claim {added} has just been added to it: {claims[added].claim}",
347	        "",
348	        "Give one arrow with that claim at one end — either end. It may cause "
349	        "something already on the map, or something already on the map may cause "
350	        "it; say which by which way round you draw it.",
351	    ]
352	    if joined:
353	        lines += ["", "It is already joined by:", *(f"  - {one}" for one in joined)]
354	    lines += [
355	        "",
356	        "Answer with that one arrow, or with a note that it is joined to this map "
357	        "as well as it needs to be.",
358	    ]
359	    return "\n".join(lines)
360	
361	
362	def expanding_question(
363	    graph: Graph,
364	    frontier: PropositionId,
365	    *,
366	    target: str | None,
367	    ending_only: bool,
368	    today: date,
369	) -> str:
370	    """Show the map as it stands, point at one claim, and ask for the next piece.
371	
372	    The varying half of every call after the first. The map is written out as
373	    sorted text so that the same map always produces the same bytes: a run can
374	    then be recorded, replayed and compared without the question drifting
375	    underneath it.
376	
377	    Nothing in here says what an earlier proposal was refused for. A claim that
378	    has just been refused is asked about again with these same bytes, which is
379	    what makes "the next call is never told why" a fact a test can check rather
380	    than a promise.
381	
382	    Args:
383	        graph: The map as it stands, including the claim being pointed at.
384	        frontier: The claim we are asking about.
385	        target: The place the person asked whether the story gets to, in their own
386	            words, or nothing at all when they did not name one.
387	        ending_only: True on the one last call a run makes when it has run out of
388	            room and the map still ends nowhere anybody could act on. It narrows
389	            the question to an ending and nothing else.
390	        today: The day this run is happening, so a claim can be given a date the
391	            answer is known by. It sits in the varying half, never in the
392	            standing half.
393	
394	    Returns:
395	        The varying half of the request, as plain text.
396	    """
397	    claims = {one.id: one for one in graph.propositions}
398	    here = claims[frontier]
399	    children = sorted(
400	        claims[arrow.target].claim for arrow in graph.links if arrow.source == frontier
401	    )
402	
403	    lines = [
404	        _today(today),
405	        "",
406	        "Here is the map as it stands. The short name in front of each claim is "
407	        "ours; use one when you name a cause.",
408	        "",
409	        _map_as_text(graph),
410	        "",
411	        f"We are asking about this claim: {here.claim}",
412	    ]
413	    if children:
414	        lines += ["", "It already leads to:", *(f"  - {child}" for child in children)]
415	    if target is not None:
416	        lines += [
417	            "",
418	            "The person wants to know whether the story reaches this:",
419	            "",
420	            f"    {target.strip()}",
421	            "",
422	            "Work towards it where the mechanism honestly goes that way, and do "
423	            "not bend a step to get there — if it does not reach, we would rather "
424	            "say so.",
425	        ]
426	    if ending_only:
427	        lines += [
428	            "",
429	            "This run has no more room to grow, and the map still ends nowhere "
430	            "anybody could act on. So this once, answer only with an ending: "
431	            "something somebody could put money on, or a plain statement that "
432	            "there is nothing to trade here and why. If neither is honest from "
433	            "this claim, say that this part of the story is finished.",
434	        ]
435	    else:
436	        if _at_the_very_start(graph, frontier):
437	            lines += ["", ASK_FOR_A_STEP_FIRST]
438	        lines += [
439	            "",
440	            "Answer with the one next piece, or with a note that this part of the "
441	            "story is finished.",
442	        ]
443	    return "\n".join(lines)
444	
445	
446	ASK_FOR_A_STEP_FIRST = (
447	    "Nothing on the map carries the story on from this claim yet, and it sits at "
448	    "the very start of the story. **A step is what would help most here**: "
449	    "something that happens on the way, which causes the next thing. A map that "
450	    "goes from the first claim straight to something you could trade has skipped "
451	    "the argument that makes the trade worth anything, and the argument is the "
452	    "whole of what we are building. If the honest next piece really is an ending, "
453	    "give that instead — and once one step leaves this claim, an ending here is "
454	    "welcome too."
455	)
456	"""What the question adds while a claim at the very start of the story has no step yet.
457	
458	**Measured, 2026-09-20.** A run on the new prompt answered the hypothesis three
459	times running with a tradeable ending — Brent, TTF, JKM — and since an ending
460	never joins the frontier, the frontier emptied and the map stopped at four claims
461	and one layer. The model was not confusing a step for an ending: the standing
462	half says what an ending *is* with more precision than it says anything else, so
463	"propose a tradeable ending" is the clearest task on offer, and nothing in the
464	varying half said it was not this call's task.
465	
466	So the correction goes in the varying half, where it costs no cached prefix and
467	can depend on the map. **It is a preference, not a rule.** Nothing in `expand.py`
468	refuses an early ending, and an ending straight off the hypothesis is sometimes
469	the right arrow — the first Opus run's `Hormuz -> Brent` was one. What this
470	stops is an early ending being the *obvious* move three times over.
471	"""
472	
473	
474	def _at_the_very_start(graph: Graph, frontier: PropositionId) -> bool:
475	    """Say whether this claim is near the start of the story and leads nowhere onward.
476	
477	    Two conditions, and both must hold. **Near the start**: the claim is the one
478	    the map began from, or one arrow away from it. **Leading nowhere onward**: no
479	    arrow out of it reaches a claim the story could carry on through — an ending
480	    is not a step, which is the whole point.
481	
482	    Args:
483	        graph: The map as it stands.
484	        frontier: The claim being asked about.
485	
486	    Returns:
487	        True while a step would help this claim more than an ending would.
488	    """
489	    kinds = {one.id: one.kind for one in graph.propositions}
490	    near_the_start = frontier == graph.hypothesis_id or any(
491	        arrow.source == graph.hypothesis_id and arrow.target == frontier for arrow in graph.links
492	    )
493	    if not near_the_start:
494	        return False
495	    return not any(
496	        arrow.source == frontier and kinds.get(arrow.target) not in TERMINAL_KINDS
497	        for arrow in graph.links
498	    )
499	
500	
501	def _map_as_text(graph: Graph) -> str:
502	    """Write the map out as one block of sorted text.
503	
504	    Sorted, so the same map is always the same bytes. Small, so the growing half
505	    of a request stays cheap: one line per claim — its short name and its
506	    sentence — and one line per arrow joining two of those names.
507	
508	    The likelihoods are deliberately left out. A model shown its own earlier
509	    numbers anchors on them, and none of them is needed to propose the next step.
510	
511	    Args:
512	        graph: The map to write out.
513	
514	    Returns:
515	        The map as plain text, claims first and then arrows.
516	    """
517	    claims = sorted(graph.propositions, key=lambda one: one.id)
518	    lines = ["Claims:"]
519	    started_at = " (this is what the person expects)"
520	    lines += [
521	        f"  {one.id}  {one.claim}" + (started_at if one.kind == "hypothesis" else "")
522	        for one in claims
523	    ]
524	    arrows = sorted(graph.links, key=lambda one: (one.source, one.target, one.id))
525	    if arrows:
526	        lines += ["", "Arrows:", *(f"  {one.source} -> {one.target}" for one in arrows)]
527	    return "\n".join(lines)
528	
529	
530	def _today(today: date) -> str:
531	    """Say what day it is, once, at the top of the varying half.
532	
533	    A person who types "next week" means a week from a particular day, and a
534	    claim's date has to be settleable against something. This is the only moving
535	    part in a request that is not the map itself, and it is deliberately below
536	    the block the service remembers: put it above and every run would pay full
537	    price for every call.
538	
539	    Args:
540	        today: The day this run is happening.
541	
542	    Returns:
543	        One line.
544	    """
545	    return f"Today is {today.isoformat()}."
